lines.say: Here's a puzzle. Can a gate change a qubit but leave the odds of reading zero or one unchanged?
Picture the qubit as an arrow. Up always reads zero, down always reads one.
The odds depend only on how far up or down it points, like latitude on a globe.
Cities on one line of latitude are equally far north, however far east or west.
That's longitude. Our arrow has one too, the way it faces round the globe, called the phase.
The Z gate spins the arrow half way round its latitude, so the odds stay put.
S turns it a quarter of the way, and T an eighth.
Let's test it. Lay the arrow on the equator pointing right, and it's fifty fifty.
Apply Z, and it swings round to point left. Still fifty fifty.
So did Z do nothing? The bars never moved, but the arrow turned.
Now add an H gate. It tips the arrow up or down, depending on which way it faces.
Without the Z, it lands straight up, and reads zero every time.
With the Z, it lands straight down, and reads one every time.
Same odds before, opposite answers after. The phase was there all along.
Here the globe breaks. Maps print longitude, but no measurement reads phase directly.
Only a later gate, like our H, turns phase into odds. That's called interference.
In the formula, theta tracks latitude, the odds, and phi tracks longitude, the phase.
So phase is the arrow's longitude: invisible now, but it decides what happens later.
